```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

hovercraft puts a tip on any HTML tag in a Shiny app or a bslib page. The tip shows when the pointer rests on the tag or
keyboard focus arrives on it, and hides when either leaves. It is plain text, or drawn from a template and filled in from
the values of one item, such as a row of a table.

```{r}
library(hovercraft)
```

## A tip with text

`tip_on()` takes a tag and the text. The text is markdown (strong, emphasis, code, links and short lists), shown as
written: build it with `paste0()` or `sprintf()` when it holds values.

```{r}
run <- tip_on(htmltools::tags$button("Run"), "Runs the **check**")
run
```

The tag comes back with the tip's attributes and the engine's script and CSS attached, so it works wherever you put it:
in a bslib page, in a plain Shiny page and in output made later with `renderUI()`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "48%", fig.alt = "A button labelled Run, with a tip below it, a shade of the page, joined to the button by a small arrow, that reads: Runs the check.", fig.show = "hold"}
knitr::include_graphics(c("figures/default-light.png", "figures/default-dark.png"))
```

The tip follows the page. On a page with a `bslib::bs_theme()` it uses the theme's colours and turns dark with
`bslib::input_dark_mode()`. See `vignette("themes")` to set its look yourself.

## A tip from a template

When many tags show the same kind of tip, write the tip once as a template and give each tag its values.

```{r}
tip_define(
  diff = tip_template(
    tip_title("{{ label }}"),
    tip_badge("{{ status }}"),
    tip_fields(Records = "{{ records | number:0 }}", Differences = "{{ differences | number:0 }}"),
    tip_text("{{ share | percent:1 }} of the records differ.")
  )
)
```

`tip_define()` returns tags: put it once in the page's UI. A template is a list of blocks, shown in order:

| Block | Shows |
|---|---|
| `tip_title()` | the first line |
| `tip_text()` | a paragraph of markdown |
| `tip_badge()` | a short label, coloured by `status =` |
| `tip_fields()` | label and value pairs |
| `tip_code()` | code, as text |

A placeholder is `{{ field }}`, or `{{ field | number:2 }}` and `{{ field | percent:1 }}` to round. It names one field of the
record, exactly, and a value that is missing or blank shows a dash. A mistake in a placeholder, such as one that never
closes, stops with an error when the template is made, not later in the browser.

A badge may say what state its item is in. `tip_badge("Check", status = "warning")` takes one of `"success"`, `"warning"`,
`"danger"` or `"info"`, and any other word is an error that lists the four. The colours come from the page's Bootstrap
colours, so they follow a bslib theme and its dark mode. Colour never carries the meaning alone: the badge's own text should
say it too.

Then name the template and give the tag a record, a named list of single values or a data frame of one row:

```{r}
row <- list(label = "ADAE", status = "Check", records = 5304, differences = 3, share = 0.0006)
tip_on(htmltools::tags$button("ADAE"), template = "diff", record = row)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "48%", fig.alt = "A button labelled ADAE, with a tip below it, joined to the button by a small arrow, holding a title, a badge, two label and value pairs and a sentence.", fig.show = "hold"}
knitr::include_graphics(c("figures/template-light.png", "figures/template-dark.png"))
```

## A short tip with a long form

`more` holds a long form that waits behind a "More" button at the bottom of the tip. The button opens the long form in
the same tip, and "Less" closes it again. The tip stays open, on its side, and grows away from the item; with the focus on
the item or the pointer resting on it, the `M` key does the same as the button, except in a text field. The next time the tip opens it is short again,
and a pinned tip has the same buttons. Nothing needs a pin or an `id`. `tip_more(on = "click")` opens the long form on a
click of the item instead (not on a control), and `tip_more(pin = TRUE)` makes the button pin the tip too, so the long
form stays:

```{r}
tip_on(
  htmltools::tags$button("Run"),
  "Runs the **check**",
  more = "Checks every column and prints a summary. Takes about a minute on the full data."
)
```

`tip_more()` (experimental) chooses when the long form shows: `on = "hover"` shows it with the short one, `on = "pin"`
shows it when the tip is pinned (the tag then needs a `pin` and an `id`), and `label =` changes the words of the
buttons. A pinned tip that grows sends `input$<id>_pin` with `state = "updated"`; a hover tip that grows sends nothing.

## A tip on every row of a table

Give each row of a data frame to `tip_on()` as its record: `data[i, ]` is a data frame of one row, which a record may be.
Once the template is defined, only the columns it names are kept, so nothing else in the data is written into the page:

```{r}
files <- data.frame(
  label = c("ADAE", "ADSL"),
  status = c("Check", "Same"),
  records = c(5304, 306),
  differences = c(3, 0),
  share = c(0.0006, 0),
  reviewer = c("A. Reviewer", "B. Reviewer")
)
rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(files)), function(i) {
  tip_on(
    htmltools::tags$tr(htmltools::tags$td(files$label[[i]]), tabindex = "0"),
    template = "diff",
    record = files[i, ]
  )
})
length(rows)
```

Once `tip_define()` has seen a template, `tip_on()` keeps only the columns it names, so a record that holds more is not
written out in full. A record that holds a value a tip cannot show, such as a list or a data frame, is an error that says which.

A template needs no `tip_define()` when it is only used here: give `template` a `tip_template()` and it travels with the
tag, with its fields checked against the record. Plain `text` takes placeholders too once there is a record:

```{r}
tip_on(
  htmltools::tags$button("ADAE"),
  "{{ differences }} differences in {{ records }} records",
  record = files[1, ]
)
```

Without a record the braces stay as written.

## Putting a tip on a tag again

A second `tip_on()` on a tag replaces its tip whole: the words, look, `id`, `events`, `pin` and `when_disabled` of the
first call are gone, and the new call says what it needs. When the old tip had an `id`, `events` or a pin and the new
call names none of them, `tip_on()` warns once (class `hovercraft_warning_retip`). A tag with a `title` attribute keeps
it, so the browser's own tooltip shows beside the tip; `tip_on()` warns (class `hovercraft_warning_title`) and asks you
to remove the `title`. `tip_on()` takes one tag: to tip a tab, tip the tag that is its title and give the tab a value,
`nav_panel(title = tip_on(span("Data"), "..."), value = "data")`.

## Keyboard users

A tip shows on keyboard focus, so a tag that cannot take focus, such as a table row or a `div`, gives a keyboard user no
way to its tip. `tip_on()` looks at the tag and at everything inside it, so the `div` that Shiny puts around an input is
fine, and says so once for a tag with nothing focusable in it. It never adds a tab stop itself, because a table of 3,000
rows would become 3,000 Tab stops: give the tags worth a stop `tabindex = "0"`, as above, or put the tip on a button or a link.
The rows, cells and headers of a `DT::datatable()` or `reactable::reactable()` table are the exception: `tip_table()` gives the table one tab stop and
moves between them with the arrow keys.

A button that holds only an icon has no name for a screen reader. When its tip is plain text and the button has no
`aria-label` of its own, `tip_on()` uses the tip's words, without the markdown marks, as the label:

```{r}
tip_on(htmltools::tags$button(htmltools::tags$i(class = "icon-gear")), "Open the **settings**")
```

The tip is then read once, as the button's name; the engine does not also add it as a description.

## In a Shiny app

```r
library(shiny)
library(hovercraft)

ui <- bslib::page_fluid(
  tip_define(hint = tip_template(tip_title("{{ label }}"), tip_text("{{ n }} files"))),
  uiOutput("buttons")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$buttons <- renderUI({
    tip_on(actionButton("go", "Go"), template = "hint", record = list(label = "Go", n = 3))
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

A template belongs to the whole page. Inside a Shiny module, namespace the template name with `ns()` — for example
`tip_define(!!ns("row") := tip_template(...))` and `tip_on(..., template = ns("row"))` — so two copies of the module
keep their own templates.
